title: Orion Bar (Hubble)
caption: The Orion Bar in the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Orion Nebula · constellation Orion · about 1,500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, Hubble Space Telescope Orion Treasury Project Team, Massimo Robberto (STScI, ESA); Image Processing: Zoltan Levay (STScI), Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A diagonal ridge of gas and dust runs through the lower left quarter of this Hubble image of the Orion Nebula, among clouds of varied colour, bright white foreground stars and many red, star-like points behind them. This ridge is the Orion Bar. Intense radiation from nearby hot, young stars has sculpted it.

Scientists see the Orion Bar as probably the model example of a photodissociation region, or PDR. In such a region, ultraviolet light from young, massive stars creates a warm, mostly neutral layer that sits between the fully ionized gas around the stars and the clouds where they were born. That light breaks molecules apart, strips electrons from atoms and heats the gas.

The bar is not really a single bar. It holds four distinct zones, layered like a cake, that change with distance from the massive stars much as warmth fades away from a fireplace. When this image was released in 2021, a team planned to study those zones with the James Webb Space Telescope, then scheduled to launch in October.

understand.summary: A Hubble mosaic combining ACS visible-light and WFC3 infrared exposures. NASA shows F435W in blue, F555W in cyan, F775W in yellow and F139M in red.
understand.eye: The red channel comes from infrared light the eye cannot see, and many separate exposures were combined into one mosaic.

explore: No region of massive star formation lies closer to the Sun than the Orion Nebula. Studies of meteorites suggest the solar system formed in a similar region, so the Orion Bar is a way to learn about our own early history. Scientists also think it may resemble conditions in starburst galaxies at a time when the universe had reached roughly half of its present age.
